verse.text: The beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'gospel', which today suggests a religious term or the title of a book. In the first century the word was an ordinary one for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

note.traditional: Jesus Christ, the Son of God

verse.note: Most manuscripts continue with 'Son of God', and most English translations include it. The words are missing from a few early witnesses, including the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, and the SBLGNT text translated here omits them. Scholars are divided on whether the phrase was dropped by accident or added by a copyist.

verse.text: Just as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: “Look, I am sending my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way;
verse.note: Only the lines in verse 3 come from Isaiah (40:3). The lines in verse 2 blend Exodus 23:20 and Malachi 3:1. Many later manuscripts read 'in the prophets', probably to smooth this over, which is why older English versions have that wording.

text.q: a voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight,’”

verse.text: so John the Baptizer appeared in the wilderness, proclaiming a baptism of turning back for the forgiveness of sins.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'repentance' (and 'repent' in verse 15), which in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term understood to include a change of life.

verse.text: And the whole Judean countryside and all the people of Jerusalem were going out to him, and they were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey.

note.term: a leather belt around his waist

verse.note: The description echoes that of the prophet Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8, a hairy garment and a leather belt. A reader who knew the Scriptures would have caught the hint that John comes in the role of Elijah, whose return was expected before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5).

verse.text: And he proclaimed, “One who is stronger than I is coming after me; I am not fit to stoop down and untie the strap of his sandals.

text.q: I baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

verse.text: In those days it happened that Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized in the Jordan by John.
And at once, as he was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit, like a dove, coming down on him.
verse.note: The Greek is plural here and in verse 11, a Semitic turn of phrase that many translations flatten to 'heaven', at least in verse 11. The plural is kept in both places. The verb 'torn open' is a violent one, and may echo the plea of Isaiah 64:1 that God would tear the heavens and come down.

Mark's preposition usually means 'into' or 'to', whereas Matthew and Luke use the word for 'upon'. Some scholars take Mark to mean that the Spirit entered Jesus. In everyday Greek of the period the preposition was often used loosely for motion toward or onto something, and the image of a dove suits alighting, so the traditional sense is kept here.

verse.text: And a voice came from the heavens: “You are my Son, the beloved; in you I delight.”
And at once the Spirit drove him out into the wilderness.
He was in the wilderness forty days, being tested by Satan; he was with the wild animals, and the angels were serving him.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'tempted'. The Greek verb means to put to the test, whether with good or hostile intent, and the forty days in the wilderness recall Israel's testing there. 'Tempted' narrows this to enticement to sin, which is part of the meaning but not the whole of it.

verse.text: After John had been handed over, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the good news of God
verse.note: Most translations say John was 'arrested' or 'put in prison', which is what happened. The Greek verb is simply 'handed over', and it is the same verb Mark later uses again and again for Jesus being handed over to his death. The literal rendering lets the reader hear that link.

verse.text: and saying, “The time has been fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near. Turn back, and believe in the good news.”
verse.note: The verb can mean that the kingdom has drawn close but has not yet come, or that it has in effect arrived. Scholars dispute which is meant, and the rendering leaves the question open as the Greek does. 'Kingdom' here leans toward God's active reign more than a territory.

verse.text: As he was passing along beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, Simon’s brother, casting a net in the sea, for they were fishers.
And Jesus said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of people.”
And at once they left their nets and followed him.
Going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and his brother John, who were in their boat mending the nets,
and at once he called them. And they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and went off after him.
They went into Capernaum, and at once, on the Sabbath, he began teaching in the synagogue.
They were astounded at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes did.
verse.note: These were not copyists but trained scholars and teachers of the Law of Moses, the recognised experts in interpreting it. The contrast is between their learned teaching and Jesus's direct authority.

verse.text: Just then there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out,

text.q: “What do you want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God!”

verse.text: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!”
And the unclean spirit threw him into convulsions, cried out with a loud voice, and came out of him.
They were all so amazed that they began asking one another, “What is this? A new teaching! With authority he commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.”
And at once the report about him went out everywhere, through the whole surrounding region of Galilee.
And at once, on leaving the synagogue, they went to the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John.
Now Simon’s mother-in-law was lying down with a fever, and at once they told him about her.
He came to her, took her by the hand, and raised her up; the fever left her, and she began serving them.
When evening came, after the sun had set, people were bringing to him all who were sick and those possessed by demons,
verse.note: The day described is a Sabbath (verse 21), which ended at sunset. Carrying the sick was regarded as work forbidden on the Sabbath, so the townspeople wait until the day is over before bringing them.

verse.text: and the whole town was gathered at the door.
He healed many who were sick with various diseases and drove out many demons, and he would not let the demons speak, because they knew him.
Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he got up, went out, and went away to a deserted place, and there he was praying.
Simon and those with him tracked him down,
and when they found him they said to him, “Everyone is looking for you.”
He said to them, “Let us go elsewhere, into the neighboring towns, so that I may proclaim there too, for that is what I came out to do.”
And he went through the whole of Galilee, proclaiming in their synagogues and driving out the demons.
A man with leprosy came to him, begging him and kneeling down, and saying to him, “If you are willing, you can make me clean.”
verse.note: The Greek term covers a range of scaly skin conditions, not only the disease now called leprosy (Hansen's disease). Under Leviticus 13–14 such conditions made a person ritually unclean and excluded from the community until a priest certified recovery. This is why the man asks to be made clean, and why he is sent to the priest.

verse.text: Angered, he stretched out his hand, touched him, and said to him, “I am willing; be made clean.”
verse.note: The great majority of manuscripts read 'moved with compassion', and most English translations follow them. A few witnesses read 'angered', which the SBLGNT adopts on the ground that a copyist would more readily soften anger into compassion than the reverse. The question is disputed. If 'angered' is original, the anger is not explained and may be directed at the disease and what it has done to the man.

verse.text: And at once the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.
And warning him sternly, he sent him away at once,
saying to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”

But he went out and began to proclaim it at length and to spread the story, so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly, but stayed outside in deserted places; and people kept coming to him from everywhere.
When he came back into Capernaum some days later, word got out that he was at home.
And so many gathered that there was no longer any room, not even around the door, and he was speaking the word to them.
And some people came, bringing to him a paralyzed man carried by four of them.
And since they could not bring him to Jesus because of the crowd, they removed the roof above where he was, and when they had dug through, they lowered the mat on which the paralyzed man was lying.
verse.note: Village houses in Galilee typically had flat roofs of wooden beams overlaid with branches or reeds and packed clay, reached by an outside stair or ladder. Opening such a roof meant literally digging through it, which is the verb Mark uses.

verse.text: And seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralyzed man, “Child, your sins are forgiven.”
verse.note: Most English versions have ‘Son’. The Greek word is the ordinary word for ‘child’, used here as an affectionate address to an adult; it is not the word for ‘son’ that appears in ‘Son of Man’ in verse 10, and the rendering keeps the two distinct.

verse.text: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, reasoning in their hearts,

text.q: “Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?”

verse.note: The Greek is literally ‘except one, God’. The wording probably echoes Israel’s daily confession that God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4), which sharpens the charge: Jesus is claiming what belongs to the one God.

verse.text: And immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit that they were reasoning this way within themselves, said to them, “Why are you reasoning these things in your hearts?

text.q: Which is easier: to say to the paralyzed man, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat and walk’?

verse.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—” he said to the paralyzed man,
verse.note: This is the first occurrence in Mark of the phrase Jesus uses for himself. Behind it lies a Semitic idiom meaning ‘a human being’, and many scholars also hear an allusion to the human-like figure who is given authority in Daniel 7:13–14. How much of each sense a first hearer would have caught is disputed.

text.q: “I say to you, get up, pick up your mat and go home.”

verse.text: And he got up, and immediately picked up the mat and went out in front of everyone, so that they were all astonished and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this!”
And he went out again beside the sea, and the whole crowd kept coming to him, and he taught them.
And as he passed by, he saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he got up and followed him.
verse.note: The ‘tax collectors’ of the Gospels were mostly collectors of tolls and customs duties on goods in transit, working under contract and profiting from what they took in. Capernaum lay near a border and on a trade route, so a customs post there is plausible. Such men were widely regarded as dishonest and were shunned by the observant, which explains the pairing ‘tax collectors and sinners’ in the next verses.

verse.text: And it happened that he was reclining at table in his house, and many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many of them, and they were following him.
verse.note: The Greek does not say whose house this is. Most interpreters take it as Levi’s, as Luke 5:29 states outright; some take it as Jesus’s own home in Capernaum (compare verse 1). The translation leaves the pronoun as open as the Greek.

verse.text: And the scribes of the Pharisees, seeing that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
verse.note: Many later manuscripts read ‘the scribes and the Pharisees’, a more familiar phrase. The unusual wording translated here, meaning scribes who belonged to the Pharisaic party, is found in early witnesses and is generally judged original.

verse.text: And hearing this, Jesus said to them, “The healthy have no need of a doctor, but the sick do. I did not come to call the just, but sinners.”
verse.note: English divides a single Greek word-family between ‘just/justice’ and ‘righteous/righteousness’; this translation uses the ‘just’ family throughout so that the connection remains audible. Most versions prefer ‘righteous’ because the word often means being in right standing before God, which modern ‘just’ can narrow, and both choices lose something. Here it means people who are in the right with God, in contrast to ‘sinners’.

verse.text: Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?”
And Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast.
verse.note: The Greek is literally ‘the sons of the wedding hall’ (or ‘bridal chamber’), a Semitic idiom for those who belong to the wedding party. It may mean the guests in general or, more narrowly, the bridegroom’s attendants. A wedding was a time of feasting, at which fasting would have been out of place.

text.q: But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast, on that day.
No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment; otherwise the patch pulls away from it, the new from the old, and the tear becomes worse.
And no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wine will burst the skins, and the wine is lost, and the skins too. No—new wine into fresh wineskins.”

verse.text: And it happened that he was passing through the grainfields on the Sabbath, and his disciples began to make their way, plucking the heads of grain.
And the Pharisees said to him, “Look, why are they doing on the Sabbath what is not permitted?”
And he said to them, “Have you never read what David did when he was in need and was hungry, he and those with him—

text.q: how he went into the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the loaves of presentation, which no one is permitted to eat except the priests, and gave some also to those who were with him?”

note.term: in the time of Abiathar the high priest

verse.note: In the account in 1 Samuel 21:1–6 the priest David meets is Ahimelech, the father of Abiathar; Abiathar became the better-known priest of David’s reign. Some explain the phrase as a loose dating by the more famous figure, others as meaning ‘in the passage about Abiathar’ (compare the similar expression at Mark 12:26). The difficulty is real, and no explanation is agreed; Matthew and Luke do not have the phrase.

note.traditional: the bread of the Presence (older: the shewbread)

verse.note: The traditional ‘bread of the Presence’ translates the Hebrew expression behind the phrase. The Greek term, taken over from the Septuagint, means ‘setting out’ or ‘presentation’. It refers to the twelve loaves set out before God in the sanctuary each Sabbath, which the priests alone ate afterwards (Leviticus 24:5–9).

verse.text: And he said to them, “The Sabbath was made for people, and not people for the Sabbath;
verse.note: The traditional ‘the Sabbath was made for man’ uses ‘man’ for humanity in general, which is what the Greek word means here. The cost of ‘people’ is that English no longer shows the verbal link with ‘Son of Man’ in the next verse, where the same Greek word appears. Some scholars think the underlying saying meant that human beings are lord of the Sabbath, but Mark clearly applies the title to Jesus.

text.q: so the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”

verse.text: He went into a synagogue again, and a man was there who had a withered hand.
They were watching him closely to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they could bring a charge against him.
He said to the man with the withered hand, “Get up and stand in the middle.”
Then he said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to kill?” But they were silent.
He looked around at them with anger, deeply grieved at the hardness of their hearts, and said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
The Pharisees went out and immediately began plotting against him with the Herodians, how they might destroy him.
verse.note: The Herodians were apparently supporters of the family of Herod, here Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee under Rome. Little else is known of them. Their alliance with the Pharisees is striking, since the two groups had little in common politically or religiously.

verse.text: Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great multitude from Galilee followed; and from Judea
and from Jerusalem and from Idumea and beyond the Jordan and around Tyre and Sidon, a great multitude, hearing all that he was doing, came to him.
He told his disciples to keep a small boat ready for him because of the crowd, so that they would not crush him;
for he had healed many, so that all who had afflictions were falling upon him to touch him.
And the unclean spirits, whenever they saw him, would fall down before him and cry out, “You are the Son of God!”
And he warned them sternly not to make him known.
Then he went up the mountain and called to him those whom he himself wanted, and they came to him.
He appointed twelve, so that they would be with him and so that he could send them out to proclaim
verse.note: Some early manuscripts add “whom he also named apostles” after “twelve”; the edition translated here judges this an addition under the influence of Luke 6:13. The repeated “He appointed the twelve” in verse 16 is likewise missing from many manuscripts.

The verb describes what a herald does: making a public announcement on someone else's authority. “Preach” now suggests delivering a sermon to a congregation, so “proclaim” is used, as in several modern versions. Many translations still have “preach.”

verse.text: and to have authority to drive out the demons.
He appointed the twelve: Simon, to whom he gave the name Peter;
and James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to them he gave the name Boanerges, which means Sons of Thunder);
and Andrew and Philip and Bartholomew and Matthew and Thomas and James the son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus and Simon the Cananaean

note.traditional: Simon the Canaanite; Simon the Cananaean; Simon the Zealot

verse.note: The epithet has nothing to do with Canaan or the village of Cana. It represents an Aramaic word meaning “zealous one,” which Mark leaves untranslated and Luke renders in Greek as “the Zealot.” Whether it marks religious zeal in general or sympathy with armed resistance to Rome is uncertain.

verse.text: and Judas Iscariot, who also handed him over.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for handing someone or something over, and it is the same word used later when Jesus is handed over to the chief priests and to Pilate. Most translations render it “betrayed” when Judas is the subject, which fits what he did but hides the repeated verb. Greek had a separate word for treachery, which Mark does not use here.

verse.text: Then he went into a house, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat bread.
When his family heard of it, they went out to take hold of him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind.”

note.traditional: his friends (KJV); his family (most modern versions)

verse.note: The Greek is a vague phrase, literally “those from beside him,” which can mean relatives, associates or envoys. Most scholars take it as his relatives, because his mother and brothers arrive in verse 31. It is also possible to read “they were saying” impersonally, so that the family acts because people were saying he was out of his mind.

verse.text: And the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying, “He has Beelzebul,” and, “By the ruler of the demons he drives out the demons.”
verse.note: In the Gospels “scribes” are not copyists but trained experts in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, recognised as teachers and legal authorities. Those “from Jerusalem” carry the weight of the religious capital. Some translations render the word “teachers of the law.”

Beelzebul is a name for the chief of the demons, treated in verse 23 as equivalent to Satan. Its origin is debated; it probably goes back to a title of the Canaanite god Baal. The form “Beelzebub” in older English Bibles comes from the Latin tradition and echoes the god of Ekron in 2 Kings 1.

verse.text: So he called them to him and spoke to them in parables: “How can Satan drive out Satan?

text.q: If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.
And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand.
And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand; his end has come.
But no one can go into the strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first ties up the strong man; and then he will plunder his house.
Truly I tell you, everything will be forgiven the sons of men, the sins and the blasphemies, whatever blasphemies they utter;

verse.note: This is a Semitic idiom meaning simply human beings, men and women alike; it is the plural of the expression “son of man.” Some modern versions render it “people.” The idiom is kept here because the Greek has it.

text.q: but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin.”

verse.note: Later manuscripts replace “sin” with “judgment,” which is the source of the King James Version's “eternal damnation.” The earlier and harder reading is “sin.” The phrase means a sin whose guilt is never removed, matching “never has forgiveness” in the same sentence.

verse.text: He said this because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”
Then his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside, they sent word to him, calling for him.
A crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, “Look, your mother and your brothers are outside, looking for you.”
verse.note: Some manuscripts add “and your sisters” here. The edition translated here omits the words; other critical editions print them in brackets as doubtful. They may have been added because of “sister” in verse 35, or dropped to match verses 31 and 33–34.

verse.text: He answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?”
And looking around at those seated in a circle around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers!
verse.note: The Greek plural can include women, and this translation normally renders it “brothers and sisters” when a mixed group is meant, as the seated crowd is here. “Brothers” is kept because Jesus is repeating word for word the phrase just used of his actual mother and brothers in verses 32–33, and the echo is the point of the saying. Verse 35 then names “sister” explicitly.

text.q: For whoever does the will of God, that person is my brother and sister and mother.”

verse.text: Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered around him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, while the whole crowd was on the land beside the sea.
verse.note: This is the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about thirteen miles long. Mark calls it a 'sea', following Semitic usage in which one word covers any large body of water; Luke prefers 'lake'. 'Sea' is kept because the word carries weight at the end of the chapter, where the scene recalls Old Testament language about God ruling the sea.

verse.text: He taught them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them:

text.q: “Listen! Look, a sower went out to sow.
And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and ate it up.
Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and it sprang up at once because it had no depth of soil;
and when the sun rose it was scorched, and because it had no root it withered.
Other seed fell among the thorns, and the thorns came up and choked it, and it yielded no crop.
And other seeds fell into the good soil and yielded a crop, coming up and growing, and produced one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one a hundredfold.”

note.traditional: some thirtyfold, some sixty, some a hundred

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts were written without accents or breathing marks, so the same letters can be read as 'one' or as the preposition 'in', and some manuscripts have a different preposition altogether. The edition translated here reads 'one … one … one', probably reflecting an Aramaic idiom for '-fold'. The sense is not materially affected.

verse.text: And he said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let them hear!”
When he was alone, those around him, together with the Twelve, asked him about the parables.
And he said to them, “To you the secret of the kingdom of God has been given; but to those outside, everything comes in parables,
verse.note: The older English rendering is 'mystery', which now suggests a puzzle or something inherently unknowable. In period usage, including the Greek version of Daniel, the word means something hidden that God has disclosed to chosen recipients. Many modern translations likewise use 'secret'.

text.q: so that ‘they may look and look yet not see, and hear and hear yet not understand; otherwise they might turn back and be forgiven.’”

verse.note: The Greek conjunction most naturally expresses purpose, and the text is translated that way. Some interpreters take it as result ('with the result that') or as shorthand for 'so that the scripture might be fulfilled', and the word rendered 'otherwise' can also mean 'unless perhaps'. The question is much disputed; the parallel in Matthew 13:13 has 'because' instead.

note.term: they may look and look yet not see

verse.note: Jesus adapts Isaiah 6:9–10, where the prophet is told his preaching will meet with incomprehension. The closing words 'be forgiven' differ from the Septuagint's 'I will heal them' and agree with the Aramaic paraphrase of Isaiah used in synagogues. The doubled verbs reproduce a Hebrew idiom of emphasis.

verse.text: And he said to them, “You do not grasp this parable? Then how will you understand all the parables?

text.q: The sower sows the word.
These are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, at once Satan comes and takes away the word that was sown in them.
And these, likewise, are the ones sown on the rocky ground: when they hear the word, they at once receive it with joy,
yet they have no root in themselves and last only a while; then, when trouble or persecution comes because of the word, at once they fall away.
And others are the ones sown among the thorns. These are the ones who have heard the word,
but the worries of the age and the deceitfulness of wealth and the desires for everything else come in and choke the word, and it bears no crop.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a span of time, here the present era of human history as contrasted with the age to come, rather than the physical world. Most translations have 'world' or 'this life'. 'Age' keeps the temporal sense a first-century Jewish hearer would have recognised.

text.q: And those are the ones sown on the good soil: they hear the word and accept it and bear a crop, one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one a hundredfold.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be put under the grain measure or under the bed? Is it not to be put on the lampstand?
verse.note: The word is a borrowing of the Latin modius, a household vessel for measuring dry goods that held roughly eight or nine litres. The traditional 'bushel' names a measure about four times that size and no longer suggests a container to most readers. Modern translations vary between 'basket' and 'bowl'.

text.q: For nothing is hidden except to be brought to light, and nothing was concealed except to come to light.
If anyone has ears to hear, let them hear!”

verse.text: And he said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear. By the measure you measure with, it will be measured to you, and more will be added to you.

text.q: For whoever has will be given more; and whoever does not have, even what they have will be taken away from them.”

verse.text: And he said, “The kingdom of God is like this: as if a man were to cast seed on the ground

text.q: and sleep and rise, night and day, while the seed sprouts and grows tall, he himself does not know how.
On its own the ground bears a crop: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.
But when the crop is ready, at once he sends in the sickle, because the harvest has come.”

verse.note: The wording echoes Joel 3:13 (4:13 in the Greek numbering), 'Send in the sickle, for the harvest has come', a picture of God's final judgment. A hearer who knew the prophets would catch that the parable's harvest points to the end of the age.

verse.text: And he said, “How shall we picture the kingdom of God, or in what parable shall we put it?

text.q: It is like a mustard seed, which, when it is sown on the ground, is smaller than all the seeds on the earth—
yet when it is sown, it comes up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the sky can nest under its shade.”

note.term: the birds of the sky can nest under its shade
note.traditional: the birds of the air can make nests in its shade

verse.note: The image recalls Ezekiel 17:23 and 31:6 and Daniel 4:12, where a great tree sheltering birds stands for a kingdom that gives protection to many peoples. 'Birds of the heaven' is a standing Semitic phrase for wild birds; the visible sky is meant.

verse.text: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as far as they were able to hear it;
he did not speak to them without a parable, but privately, to his own disciples, he explained everything.
On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let us cross over to the other side.”
And leaving the crowd, they took him along in the boat, just as he was; and other boats were with him.
And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling.
But he himself was in the stern, sleeping on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?”
And he woke up, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Quiet! Be silent!” And the wind died down, and there was a great calm.
verse.note: The traditional wording sounds soothing, but the Greek is a pair of sharp commands to stop making noise. The second verb is used in the period both for muzzling an animal and for silencing a person, and it is the one Jesus uses to silence the unclean spirit in 1:25. Its form here implies 'be silenced and stay so'.

verse.text: And he said to them, “Why are you such cowards? Do you still have no faith?”
verse.note: The adjective means cowardly or timid and is a term of reproach, a different word from the ordinary one for fear used in the next verse. Most translations render 'afraid' or 'fearful', which blurs the distinction between the disciples' loss of nerve in the storm and their awe afterwards.

verse.text: And they were seized with a great fear and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
And they came to the other side of the sea, to the region of the Gerasenes.
verse.note: Manuscripts vary between Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes, here and in the parallel accounts. Gerasenes has the best early support in Mark and is the reading of the SBLGNT, but Gerasa (modern Jerash) lies more than thirty miles from the lake, which probably prompted copyists to substitute nearer places. The older English tradition, following later manuscripts, reads Gadarenes.

verse.text: As he got out of the boat, at once a man with an unclean spirit came from the tombs to meet him.
He had his dwelling among the tombs, and no one could bind him any longer, not even with a chain,
because he had often been bound with shackles and chains, and he had torn the chains apart and smashed the shackles, and no one was strong enough to subdue him.
Constantly, night and day, among the tombs and in the hills, he was crying out and gashing himself with stones.
Seeing Jesus from a distance, he ran and bowed down before him,
verse.note: The verb describes the physical act of prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a god, a king or anyone whose power is acknowledged. Older versions have 'worshipped', which in modern English implies religious devotion. Here the act is the submission of a hostile spirit to a stronger power, so most recent translations also use 'bowed down' or 'fell on his knees'.

verse.text: and crying out in a loud voice he said, “What do you want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I put you under oath by God: do not torment me!”

note.term: I put you under oath by God

verse.note: The traditional 'adjure' is accurate but no longer ordinary English. The verb means to bind someone by an oath invoking a divine name, and it is the formula exorcists themselves used to command spirits (compare Acts 19:13). The irony is that here the spirit tries to use it on Jesus.

verse.text: For he had been saying to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!”
Then he asked him, “What is your name?” And he said to him, “Legion is my name, for we are many.”
verse.note: A Latin military term borrowed into Greek. A Roman legion at full strength numbered roughly five to six thousand soldiers, so the name signals an overwhelming occupying force as well as a great number. Whether Mark intends a political allusion to Roman occupation is debated.

verse.text: And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the region.
Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside,
and they begged him, saying, “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them.”
And he gave them permission. The unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and the herd, about two thousand of them, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and were drowned in the sea.
Those who had been tending them fled and reported it in the town and in the countryside, and people came to see what it was that had happened.
They came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, the very man who had had the legion, and they were afraid.
Those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man, and told them about the pigs.
And they began to beg him to leave their territory.
As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been demon-possessed begged him that he might be with him.
He did not let him, but said to him, “Go home to your own people and report to them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.”
verse.note: In Jesus’s mouth 'the Lord' most naturally means God, as in the Septuagint. In the next verse, however, the man proclaims what 'Jesus' had done for him. Mark sets the two side by side without comment, and readers differ on how far he means to identify them.

verse.text: And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled.
verse.note: The name means 'Ten Cities' and refers to a group of Hellenistic cities lying mostly east and south-east of the Sea of Galilee. The population was largely Gentile, which explains the presence of a large herd of pigs, animals unclean to Jews. This man is the first person in Mark to proclaim Jesus in Gentile territory.

verse.text: When Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around him, and he was beside the sea.
One of the synagogue leaders, named Jairus, came, and on seeing him fell at his feet
and begged him earnestly, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.”
verse.note: The verb here and in verses 28 and 34 is the ordinary Greek word for rescuing from danger or illness, and is the same word rendered 'save' elsewhere in the New Testament. In a context of sickness a first-century reader would hear 'recover' or 'be cured', so it is rendered 'made well' in all three verses. Some translations have 'your faith has saved you' in verse 34, and Mark may intend the wider sense to be heard.

verse.text: So he went with him. A large crowd was following him and pressing in on him.
Now there was a woman who had had a flow of blood for twelve years.
verse.note: The phrase echoes the Septuagint wording of Leviticus 15, where a woman with a prolonged discharge of blood is ritually unclean, as is anything or anyone she touches. For twelve years the condition would have restricted her participation in ordinary religious and social life. This explains both her covert approach and her fear when discovered.

verse.text: She had suffered much under many doctors and had spent everything she had, and she was no better but had instead grown worse.
Having heard about Jesus, she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his cloak,
for she had been saying, “If I touch even his clothes, I will be made well.”
And at once the source of her bleeding dried up, and she knew in her body that she had been healed of her affliction.
And at once Jesus, aware in himself that power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd and said, “Who touched my clothes?”
His disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing in on you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”
But he kept looking around to see the woman who had done this.
And the woman, frightened and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before him and told him the whole truth.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be healthy, free of your affliction.”
While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue leader’s house, saying, “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any further?”
But Jesus, disregarding what was being said, told the synagogue leader, “Do not be afraid; only believe.”
verse.note: The verb can mean either 'overhear' or 'refuse to heed'. Most modern translations choose 'overhearing', and the parallel in Luke 8:50 has simply 'hearing'. The rendering here follows the sense the word has in the Septuagint and in its only other New Testament occurrence (Matthew 18:17). Either way, Jesus hears the message and refuses to let it stand.

verse.text: And he did not let anyone accompany him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James.
They came to the synagogue leader’s house, and he saw a commotion, with people weeping and wailing loudly,
and going in he said to them, “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child has not died but is sleeping.”
And they laughed at him. But he put them all out, took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him, and went in where the child was.
Taking the child by the hand, he said to her, “Talitha koum,” which is translated, “Girl, I say to you, get up.”
verse.note: Mark preserves Jesus’s words in Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee, and then translates them for his Greek-speaking readers. The phrase means 'girl, get up'; 'I say to you' is added in Mark’s Greek translation. Many later manuscripts read 'koumi', the grammatically feminine form, which is the source of the traditional 'cumi'.

verse.text: And at once the girl stood up and began walking around, for she was twelve years old. And at once they were overcome with great amazement.
He gave them strict orders that no one should know of this, and said that she should be given something to eat.
He left there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him.

When the Sabbath came, he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astounded, saying, “Where did this man get these things? What is this wisdom that has been given to him, and what are these deeds of power done through his hands?
Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And aren’t his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him.
verse.note: The Greek word names a craftsman who builds, most often in wood but sometimes in stone. The traditional 'carpenter' is kept, though 'builder' or 'woodworker' would be equally defensible. Identifying a man by his mother rather than his father was unusual; whether the townspeople mean it as a slight is debated.

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household.”
And he could not do any deed of power there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them.
And he was amazed at their unbelief. Then he went around the surrounding villages, teaching.
He called the twelve to him and began to send them out two by two, and he gave them authority over the unclean spirits.
He instructed them to take nothing for the road except a staff alone: no bread, no bag, no money in their belts,
but to wear sandals, and not to put on two tunics.
And he said to them, “Wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave that place.

text.q: And whatever place does not welcome you, and they refuse to listen to you, as you leave there shake off the dust that is under your feet as a testimony against them.”

verse.note: The Greek says only 'as a testimony to them'. This can mean evidence against them or a warning addressed to them, and most translations choose 'against'. Shaking a place's dust from one's feet was a gesture of breaking off all association with it.

verse.text: So they went out and proclaimed that people should turn back,
verse.note: The traditional 'repent' now suggests mainly feeling sorry. In the Gospels the word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand to include a changed life.

verse.text: and they drove out many demons, and anointed many sick people with oil and healed them.
King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’s name had become well known, and people were saying, “John the Baptizer has been raised from the dead, and that is why the powers are at work in him.”
verse.note: This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome with the lesser title of tetrarch. He was never formally a king. Mark's 'king' probably reflects popular local usage, though some read it as ironic.

Here and in verse 24 Mark uses a participle, 'the one who baptizes', and in verse 25 the noun that became the fixed title 'the Baptist'. The translation keeps the difference. Most English versions print 'the Baptist' throughout.

verse.text: But others were saying, “He is Elijah,” and others were saying, “A prophet, like one of the prophets.”
But when Herod heard of it, he said, “John, the man I beheaded, has been raised!”
For Herod himself had sent men and arrested John and bound him in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, because he had married her.
For John had been telling Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
So Herodias held a grudge against him and wanted to kill him, but she could not,
for Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he listened to him he was greatly perplexed, and yet he liked to listen to him.
verse.note: English divides one Greek word-family between 'just' and 'righteous'; this translation uses 'just' and 'justice' throughout so the family stays visible. Most translations use 'righteous', which better suggests right standing before God but hides the link to ordinary justice. Both words lose something.

Many later manuscripts read a similar-looking verb, giving 'he did many things', which is the reading behind the King James Version. The earliest witnesses read 'he was greatly perplexed', which most modern editions and translations follow.

verse.text: Then an opportune day came, when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles, his military commanders, and the leading men of Galilee.
Herodias’s own daughter came in and danced, and she pleased Herod and his dinner guests. The king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you want, and I will give it to you.”
verse.note: The manuscripts are divided here. Some early and important ones read 'his daughter Herodias', which makes the girl Herod's daughter and gives her the same name as her mother; some critical editions print that reading. The text translated here makes her the daughter of Herodias, which agrees with Matthew's account. The Jewish historian Josephus names Herodias's daughter by her earlier marriage as Salome; Mark does not name her.

verse.text: And he swore to her, “Whatever you ask me I will give you, up to half my kingdom.”

note.traditional: unto the half of my kingdom

verse.note: The phrase echoes the Persian king's offer to Esther in the book of Esther and was a byword for extravagant generosity. As a ruler who held his territory at Rome's pleasure, Antipas had no kingdom he could actually give away.

verse.text: She went out and said to her mother, “What should I ask for?” She said, “The head of John the Baptizer.”
At once she hurried back in to the king and made her request: “I want you to give me, right now, on a platter, the head of John the Baptist.”
The king was deeply distressed, yet because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to refuse her.
So at once the king sent an executioner and ordered him to bring John’s head. He went and beheaded him in the prison,
brought his head on a platter, and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother.
When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his corpse and laid it in a tomb.
The apostles gathered around Jesus and reported to him all that they had done and all that they had taught.
He said to them, “Come away by yourselves to a deserted place and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no chance even to eat.
So they went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.
But many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there together on foot from all the towns and arrived ahead of them.
When he came ashore he saw a large crowd, and he felt compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.
When the hour was already late, his disciples came to him and said, “This is a deserted place, and the hour is already late.

text.q: Send them away, so that they can go to the surrounding farms and villages and buy themselves something to eat.”

verse.text: But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” They said to him, “Are we to go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?”
verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day's pay for a laborer. Two hundred denarii is therefore more than half a year's wages.

verse.text: He said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” When they had found out, they said, “Five, and two fish.”
Then he ordered them to have everyone recline, party by party, on the green grass.
And they lay down, plot by plot, in hundreds and in fifties.
verse.note: The Greek word means a garden bed, and Mark doubles it ('plots plots'), just as he doubles the word for a dining party in verse 39. The picture is of orderly rectangles of people laid out on the grass like beds in a garden. Most translations flatten both expressions to 'in groups'.

verse.text: Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, said the blessing, and broke the loaves, and he kept giving them to his disciples to set before the people; and he divided the two fish among them all.
They all ate and were satisfied,
and they picked up broken pieces, twelve basketfuls, and some of the fish as well.
Those who had eaten the loaves were five thousand men.
At once he made his disciples get into the boat and go on ahead to the other side, toward Bethsaida, while he himself dismissed the crowd.
After taking leave of them, he went off to the mountain to pray.
When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and he was alone on the land.
He saw them hard pressed at the oars, for the wind was against them, and about the fourth watch of the night he came toward them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them,

note.term: the fourth watch of the night
note.traditional: the fourth watch of the night

verse.note: By Roman reckoning the night was divided into four watches. The fourth was the last, roughly three to six in the morning, so the disciples had been rowing most of the night.

note.term: He meant to pass by them
note.traditional: he would have passed by them

verse.note: The Greek says plainly that he wanted or intended to pass by them, which puzzles many readers. A widely held view is that 'pass by' echoes the language of Israel's Scriptures for God passing by to reveal himself, as to Moses and Elijah, so that the intent is to show himself and not to avoid them. Others take it as how things looked to the disciples: 'he seemed about to pass them'.

verse.text: but when they saw him walking on the sea, they thought it was a ghost and cried out,
for they all saw him and were terrified. But at once he spoke with them and said, “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.”
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'I am'. It is the ordinary way to say 'It's me', and that is its surface meaning here. It is also the phrase the Greek Scriptures use for God's self-declaration, and in a scene of walking on the sea many interpreters hear that overtone as well; how much Mark intends it is disputed.

verse.text: Then he climbed into the boat with them, and the wind died down. And they were utterly astonished within themselves,
for they had not understood about the loaves; rather, their hearts had been hardened.
When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored there.
When they got out of the boat, people at once recognized him
and ran about that whole region and began to carry those who were ill around on their mats to wherever they heard he was.
And wherever he went, into villages or towns or farms, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged him to let them touch even the fringe of his cloak; and all who touched it were made well.

note.traditional: the border of his garment / the hem of his garment

verse.note: The word can mean simply the edge of a garment. It is also the term the Greek Scriptures use for the tassels that the Law told Israelite men to wear on the corners of their cloaks. Either may be meant here; 'fringe' leaves both possible.

verse.text: The Pharisees gathered around him, along with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem,
and they saw that some of his disciples were eating their bread with defiled hands, that is, unwashed.
verse.note: The Greek word is literally 'common', used in Jewish Greek for what is ordinary and so not ritually pure. The issue is ritual purity, not hygiene. Mark's gloss 'that is, unwashed' and the explanation in verses 3 and 4 suggest he expected readers unfamiliar with Jewish practice.

verse.text: For the Pharisees, and indeed all the Jews, do not eat unless they wash their hands with the fist, holding to the tradition of the elders;
verse.note: The Greek says literally 'with a fist', and what that meant is not known. Proposals include washing with a cupped hand, with a fistful of water, up to the wrist, or by rubbing the fist in the other palm. Many translations paraphrase with 'carefully' or 'ceremonially', and some manuscripts read 'often' instead. The literal wording is kept because none of the explanations is certain.

verse.text: and when they come from the marketplace they do not eat unless they wash themselves. And there are many other things that they have received to hold to: the washing of cups and pitchers and copper vessels and dining couches.
verse.note: The verb is the one elsewhere rendered 'baptize', and the related noun stands behind 'washing' later in the verse. Here both refer to Jewish ritual washing, possibly by immersion. The clause may also mean that they do not eat anything from the marketplace unless they wash it. Some early manuscripts read 'sprinkle' instead.
Several important early manuscripts lack these words. SBLGNT includes them, and they are translated here. The Greek word can mean a bed or a couch for reclining at meals.

verse.text: So the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat their bread with defiled hands?”
He said to them, “Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away from me.

text.q: In vain they worship me, teaching human precepts as doctrines.’
You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “How well you set aside the commandment of God in order to keep your own tradition!

text.q: For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever speaks evil of father or mother must surely die.’

verse.text: But you say that if a person tells his father or mother, ‘Whatever benefit you might have had from me is Corban’ — that is, an offering —
verse.note: Corban is a Hebrew term for something dedicated to God as an offering, which Mark translates for his readers. Declaring property Corban was a vow that put it beyond another person's use. Jesus's charge is that the vow was upheld even when it deprived parents of the support owed them under the commandment to honor them. The details of how such vows worked in this period are only partly known.

text.q: then you no longer let him do anything for his father or mother,
making void the word of God by your tradition, which you have handed down. And you do many things like that.”

verse.text: Calling the crowd to him again, he said to them, “Listen to me, all of you, and understand.

text.q: Nothing that goes into a person from outside is able to defile them; rather, the things that come out of a person are what defile the person.”

verse.note: Verse 16 ('If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear') is absent from important early manuscripts and is not in the SBLGNT text, so the numbering passes from 15 to 17. Most scholars regard it as a later addition modelled on similar sayings elsewhere in Mark.

verse.text: When he had gone into a house, away from the crowd, his disciples asked him about the parable.
He said to them, “So you too are without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile them,
because it goes not into the heart but into the stomach, and goes out into the latrine?” In saying this, he declared all foods clean.

note.term: In saying this, he declared all foods clean.

verse.note: The Greek is a participle, literally 'cleansing all foods'. In the earliest manuscripts its form is masculine and is most naturally read as the narrator's comment on what Jesus's words imply, which is the view of most modern scholars and translations. Later manuscripts have a neuter form that makes the phrase part of Jesus's sentence, describing digestion, as in the King James Version.

verse.text: And he went on, “What comes out of a person, that is what defiles the person.

text.q: For from within, out of the human heart, come evil designs: sexual immorality, thefts, murders,
adulteries, acts of greed and wickedness, deceit, debauchery, an envious eye, slander, arrogance, folly.

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'an evil eye'. In Jewish idiom this meant a grudging, envious or stingy attitude toward others, not the curse-casting glance the English phrase now suggests. Many modern translations simply put 'envy'; this rendering keeps the eye of the idiom while giving its sense.

text.q: All these wicked things come from within and defile the person.”

verse.text: From there he set out and went away to the region of Tyre. He entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not escape notice.
Instead, a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard about him at once, and she came and fell at his feet.
Now the woman was a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth, and she kept asking him to drive the demon out of her daughter.
verse.note: 'Greek' here marks the woman as a non-Jew of Greek language and culture, not as a native of Greece; some translations put 'a Gentile'. 'Syrophoenician' places her origin in Phoenicia, the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon, which belonged to the Roman province of Syria.

verse.text: He said to her, “Let the children first eat their fill, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs.”
verse.note: The Greek word is a diminutive of 'dog'. Some scholars take it to mean household dogs or puppies, which suits the picture of dogs under the table and softens the saying. Others point out that diminutives had often lost their force in Koine, and that Mark uses many, and so render simply 'dogs'. Either way the saying puts the 'children', Israel, ahead of Gentiles, and the woman accepts the image and turns it to her advantage.

verse.text: But she answered him, “Sir, even the little dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs.”
verse.note: The Greek address can be an ordinary polite 'sir' or the title 'Lord'. On the lips of a Gentile stranger the polite sense is the more likely, though Mark's Christian readers may well have heard more in it. Some manuscripts read 'Yes, Lord'.

verse.text: And he said to her, “Because of what you have said, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter.”
She went away to her home and found the child lying on the bed and the demon gone.
Then he left the region of Tyre again and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the middle of the region of the Decapolis.
They brought him a man who was deaf and could hardly speak, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.

note.traditional: had an impediment in his speech

verse.note: The Greek word is very rare. In the Greek Old Testament it appears in Isaiah 35:6, in a passage promising that the ears of the deaf will be opened and the tongue of those who can hardly speak will be made clear. Mark's choice of word, together with the crowd's words in verse 37, probably points the reader to that promise.

verse.text: Taking him aside from the crowd, in private, he put his fingers into the man’s ears, and after spitting he touched his tongue.
Then, looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened.”
verse.note: Mark preserves the word in Jesus's own language and then translates it, as he does with a few other sayings. It is usually identified as Aramaic, though some have argued it is Hebrew.

verse.text: And his ears were opened, the bond on his tongue was loosed, and he began to speak clearly.
He ordered them to tell no one; but the more he ordered them, all the more they kept proclaiming it.
They were astonished beyond all measure, saying, “He has done everything well; he even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak.”
In those days, when there was again a large crowd and they had nothing to eat, he called the disciples to him and said to them,

text.q: “I feel compassion for the crowd, because they have stayed with me three days now and have nothing to eat.
And if I send them home hungry, they will collapse on the way; and some of them have come from far away.”

verse.text: His disciples answered him, “Where could anyone get enough bread to satisfy these people, here in a deserted place?”
He asked them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven.”

He directed the crowd to recline on the ground. Then he took the seven loaves, gave thanks, broke them, and kept giving them to his disciples to set before the people, and they set them before the crowd.
They also had a few small fish; and after blessing them, he said that these too should be set before them.
They ate and were satisfied, and they picked up the leftover pieces, seven large baskets.
verse.note: Mark uses a different word for the baskets here than in the feeding of the five thousand (6:43), and Jesus keeps the two words apart when he recalls both meals in verses 19–20. This word names a hamper that could be big enough to hold a person (Acts 9:25). Most translations render both words simply as 'baskets'; 'large baskets' keeps the distinction visible, though the exact size is not certain.

verse.text: There were about four thousand. And he sent them away.
And immediately he got into the boat with his disciples and went to the region of Dalmanutha.
verse.note: This place name appears nowhere else in ancient literature and its location is unknown. Matthew's parallel has 'Magadan', and some manuscripts of Mark substitute that or 'Magdala'. It was presumably on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.

verse.text: The Pharisees came out and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from heaven, testing him.
Sighing deeply in his spirit, he said, “Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.”

note.term: no sign will be given to this generation

verse.note: The Greek literally says 'if a sign shall be given to this generation', leaving the sentence unfinished. This mirrors a Hebrew oath formula, familiar from the Greek Old Testament, in which the unspoken ending is a self-curse ('may such-and-such happen to me if ...'). It is an emphatic denial, stronger than a plain 'no'.

verse.text: And leaving them, he got into the boat again and went away to the other side.
They had forgotten to take bread, and apart from one loaf they had none with them in the boat.
And he was cautioning them, saying, “Watch out! Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.”
verse.note: Leaven was a piece of fermented dough kept back to raise the next batch, and it was a common image for an influence, usually a corrupting one, that spreads unseen through the whole. Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who had executed John the Baptist. The disciples take the remark literally, as a comment on their lack of bread.

verse.text: And they were discussing with one another that they had no bread.

note.traditional: It is because we have no bread

verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'we have no bread', giving the disciples' words directly, and many translations follow them. The text translated here reads 'they have', which reports the content of their discussion indirectly. The sense of the scene is the same either way.

verse.text: Aware of this, he said to them, “Why are you discussing that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Is your heart hardened?

text.q: Having eyes, do you not see, and having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember?

verse.text: When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of pieces did you pick up?” They said to him, “Twelve.”
“And the seven for the four thousand—how many large baskets full of pieces did you pick up?” And they said to him, “Seven.”
And he said to them, “Do you not yet understand?”
They came to Bethsaida. And people brought a blind man to him and begged him to touch him.
Taking the blind man by the hand, he led him out of the village; and after spitting on his eyes and laying his hands on him, he asked him, “Do you see anything?”
He looked up and said, “I see people—I see them like trees, walking around.”
verse.note: The Greek verb can mean either 'look up' or 'regain sight', and it has the second meaning elsewhere in Mark (10:51–52). Here 'looked up' fits the sequence better, since full sight is restored only in the next verse, but 'beginning to see again' is also possible.

verse.text: Then he laid his hands on his eyes again; and the man looked hard and was restored, and he could see everything clearly.
And he sent him to his home, saying, “Do not even go into the village.”

note.term: Do not even go into the village
note.traditional: Neither go into the town, nor tell it to any in the town

verse.note: The manuscripts differ considerably here. Many add 'nor tell anyone in the village', and others have still longer forms. The short reading translated here is found in the earliest witnesses and is the one most editors accept.

verse.text: Jesus and his disciples went out to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?”
They told him, “John the Baptist; and others, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets.”
And he asked them, “But you—who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Messiah.”
verse.note: The Greek word translates the Hebrew for 'anointed one' and here is a title: the anointed king Israel was waiting for. 'Christ' now reads as a name, so 'Messiah' is used where the title itself is the point. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

verse.text: And he sternly warned them to tell no one about him.
verse.note: The verb here is the same one translated 'rebuke' in verses 32 and 33, where Peter rebukes Jesus and Jesus rebukes Peter. Mark also uses it for Jesus silencing unclean spirits. Followed by a command, as here, it means to warn or order sternly, but a Greek reader would hear the same forceful word three times in four verses.

verse.text: Then he began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes, and be killed, and after three days rise again.
He was saying this openly. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him.
But he turned, looked at his disciples, and rebuked Peter, saying, “Get behind me, Satan! For your mind is not on the things of God but on the things of people.”
Then he called the crowd to him along with his disciples and said to them, “If anyone wants to come behind me, let them deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow me.
verse.note: The Greek phrase is the same one used in the command to Peter in verse 33, 'Get behind me.' To walk behind a teacher was the position of a disciple, so Peter is being sent back to his place as a follower, and the invitation here describes that place. Most translations have 'come after me', which hides the echo.

text.q: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake and for the sake of the good news will save it.

verse.note: The same Greek word runs through verses 35–37. Many translations switch from 'life' to 'soul' at verse 36, which breaks the argument and suggests a distinct immaterial part of a person. In the usage of the period, shaped by the Greek Old Testament, the word means a person's life or very self. 'Life' is kept throughout, as in some modern versions.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' has become a religious term and a book title, so 'good news' is used instead. Many modern translations already alternate between the two.

text.q: For what does it benefit a person to gain the whole world and forfeit their life?
For what could a person give in exchange for their life?

For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of that person when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will certainly not taste death until they see that the kingdom of God has come with power.”
After six days Jesus took Peter, James and John and led them up a high mountain by themselves, alone. And he was transformed in front of them,
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for a change of form or appearance, and Paul uses it for the change in believers (Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 3:18), where it is normally translated 'transformed'. 'Transfigured' comes from the Latin translation and is now used in English almost only for this event. Most translations keep 'transfigured'; the plain word is used here because it is what a Greek reader heard.

verse.text: and his clothes became dazzling white, far whiter than any launderer on earth could make them.
And Elijah appeared to them with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.
Peter spoke up and said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents: one for you, one for Moses and one for Elijah.”
verse.note: The word means a tent or temporary shelter. It is the Septuagint's word both for the wilderness tabernacle and for the booths of the autumn Feast of Booths, so Peter's proposal may carry festival or wilderness overtones. Why he offers it is not explained; Mark says only that he did not know what to say.

verse.text: For he did not know what to say, because they were terrified.
Then a cloud came and overshadowed them, and a voice came from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son. Listen to him.”
Suddenly, when they looked around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus alone.
As they were coming down from the mountain, he ordered them to tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.
They kept the matter to themselves, discussing what this rising from the dead meant.

note.term: They kept the matter to themselves

verse.note: The Greek phrase 'to themselves' can go with either verb. The alternative reading is 'They held on to what he said, discussing among themselves what this rising from the dead meant.' Both are grammatical and translations are divided.

verse.text: And they asked him, “Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
verse.note: The expectation rests on the closing lines of Malachi, where God promises to send the prophet Elijah before the day of the Lord. Having just seen Elijah on the mountain, the disciples ask how this fits. Jesus' answer that Elijah 'has indeed come' and was mistreated is generally understood to point to John the Baptist, as Matthew's parallel says outright.

verse.text: He said to them, “Elijah does come first and restores all things. Yet how is it written of the Son of Man that he must suffer much and be treated with contempt?

text.q: But I tell you that Elijah has indeed come, and they did to him whatever they wished, just as it is written of him.”

verse.text: When they came to the disciples, they saw a large crowd around them and scribes arguing with them.
As soon as the whole crowd saw him, they were struck with amazement and ran up to greet him.
He asked them, “What are you arguing about with them?”
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts carried no breathing marks, and here the pronoun can be read either as 'them' or as a reflexive, 'among yourselves'. The SBLGNT prints the reflexive form; most editions and translations read 'with them', which matches verse 14 and is followed here. It is also unclear whether Jesus is addressing the crowd, the scribes or the disciples.

verse.text: One of the crowd answered him, “Teacher, I brought my son to you. He has a mute spirit,

text.q: and wherever it seizes him it throws him down, and he foams at the mouth, grinds his teeth and goes rigid. I asked your disciples to drive it out, and they could not.”

verse.text: In reply he said to them, “O unbelieving generation, how long will I be with you? How long will I put up with you? Bring him to me.”
So they brought the boy to him. When the spirit saw Jesus, it at once threw the boy into convulsions, and he fell to the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth.
Jesus asked his father, “How long has this been happening to him?” He said, “From childhood.

text.q: It has often thrown him into fire and into water to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.”

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “‘If you can’! All things are possible for the one who believes.”
verse.note: In the earliest text Jesus picks up the father's own words from verse 22 and throws them back as an exclamation. Later manuscripts added 'believe', which produces the familiar older rendering 'If you can believe, all things are possible'. Modern editions and translations follow the shorter text.

verse.text: At once the child’s father cried out, “I believe; help my unbelief!”
When Jesus saw that a crowd was quickly gathering, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, “Mute and deaf spirit, I command you: come out of him and never enter him again.”
It cried out, convulsed him violently and came out. The boy became like a corpse, so that most of them said he was dead.
But Jesus took him by the hand and raised him, and he stood up.
When Jesus had gone indoors, his disciples asked him privately, “Why could we not drive it out?”
He said to them, “This kind can come out by nothing except prayer.”
verse.note: Most later manuscripts read 'by prayer and fasting'. A small number of early and important witnesses lack 'and fasting', and the SBLGNT, like most modern editions, judges the words a later addition reflecting church practice. The decision is not unanimous among scholars, since the manuscript support for the longer reading is very wide.

verse.text: They left that place and were passing through Galilee, and he did not want anyone to know,
for he was teaching his disciples and telling them, “The Son of Man is being handed over into human hands, and they will kill him, and after he has been killed, three days later he will rise.”
But they did not understand what he said, and they were afraid to ask him.
They came to Capernaum. When he was in the house, he asked them, “What were you discussing on the way?”
But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest.
He sat down, called the Twelve and said to them, “If anyone wants to be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.”
Then he took a child and stood it among them, and taking it in his arms he said to them,

text.q: “Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me; and whoever welcomes me welcomes not me but the one who sent me.”

verse.text: John said to him, “Teacher, we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.”
But Jesus said, “Do not stop him, for no one who does a work of power in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me.

text.q: For whoever is not against us is for us.
For whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ, truly I tell you, he will certainly not lose his reward.
And whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.

verse.note: The Greek specifies a 'donkey millstone': the large upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey, as opposed to a small hand mill. The point is its crushing weight.

text.q: If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go away into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire.

verse.note: Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which had become in Jewish usage a name for the place of final judgment. 'Hell' merges it with Hades, the realm of the dead, and with much later imagery. Many translations still use 'hell', usually with a footnote giving Gehenna; several modern ones keep the name.

text.q: And if your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than, having two feet, to be thrown into Gehenna.
And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than, having two eyes, to be thrown into Gehenna,
where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.

note.term: where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched

verse.note: The words echo the last verse of Isaiah (66:24), which describes the corpses of those who rebelled against God. Later manuscripts repeat this sentence after verses 43 and 45, where older English Bibles number it as verses 44 and 46. The earliest witnesses have it only here, so modern editions omit those two verses and the numbering skips them.

text.q: For everyone will be salted with fire.

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add 'and every sacrifice will be salted with salt', an echo of Leviticus 2:13, probably added to explain a difficult saying. The meaning of the short form is disputed. Common suggestions are that fire stands for testing or purifying that every disciple must undergo, or for judgment, with salt recalling its use on sacrifices.

text.q: Salt is good; but if the salt becomes unsalty, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”

verse.text: He set out from there and came into the region of Judea and across the Jordan. Crowds again gathered around him, and, as his custom was, he again taught them.
And people asked him, to test him, whether a man is allowed to divorce his wife.

note.traditional: Pharisees came up and asked him

verse.note: Most manuscripts, and most English versions, begin this verse with 'Pharisees came up and asked him.' The SBLGNT follows a smaller group of witnesses that lack these words, leaving the questioners unnamed. The longer reading may have been carried over from the parallel in Matthew 19:3. Either way, the question is presented as a test.

verse.text: He answered them, “What did Moses command you?”
They said, “Moses permitted a man to write a certificate of dismissal and divorce her.”
But Jesus said to them, “It was because of your hardness of heart that he wrote this commandment for you.

text.q: But from the beginning of creation, ‘male and female he made them.’
‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united with his wife,
and the two will become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh.
Therefore what God has joined together, no human being is to separate.”

verse.text: Back in the house, the disciples asked him about this again.
He said to them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her,

text.q: and if she herself divorces her husband and marries another man, she commits adultery.”

verse.note: In Jewish practice of the period divorce was ordinarily the husband's act, while Roman law allowed a wife to end a marriage.
