This clause, which only Mark has, addresses that second situation. The words 'against her' in the previous verse are also striking, since adultery was conventionally reckoned an offence against a husband, not against a wife.

verse.text: People were bringing little children to him so that he might touch them, but the disciples rebuked them.
When Jesus saw this, he was indignant and said to them, “Let the little children come to me; do not stop them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.

text.q: Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will never enter it.”

verse.note: The Greek form can be read as subject or object. The saying may mean 'as a little child receives it' or 'as one receives a little child'. Most interpreters take the first, and the English wording leaves the same openness as the Greek.

verse.text: And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
As he was setting out on the road, a man ran up, knelt before him, and asked him, “Good teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' meant the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as length. Verse 30 makes the link explicit: 'in the age to come, eternal life.' A minority of translators render the phrase 'life of the age to come' throughout.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one: God.

text.q: You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not give false testimony, do not defraud, honor your father and mother.’”

verse.text: He said to him, “Teacher, all these I have kept since my youth.”
Jesus looked at him and loved him, and said to him, “One thing you lack: go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”
But his face fell at these words, and he went away grieving, for he had many possessions.
Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How hard it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!”
The disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God!

note.term: how hard it is to enter the kingdom of God
note.traditional: how hard is it for them that trust in riches to enter into the kingdom of God

verse.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add 'for those who trust in riches' here. The earliest witnesses lack the words, and most editors regard them as a later softening. Without them the saying is general: entering the kingdom is hard for anyone.

text.q: It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

verse.note: The saying is a deliberate exaggeration, setting the largest animal of the region against the smallest familiar opening. The popular explanation that 'the Needle's Eye' was a small gate in Jerusalem has no ancient support and appears only in much later tradition. The disciples' reaction in the next verse shows they took it as an impossibility.

verse.text: They were utterly astounded and said to one another, “Then who can be saved?”
Jesus looked at them and said, “With people it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God.”
Peter began to say to him, “Look, we have left everything and followed you.”
Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or fields for my sake and for the sake of the good news
verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'gospel', which today suggests a religious term or the title of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

text.q: who will not receive a hundred times as much now in this present time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and fields, with persecutions, and in the age to come, eternal life.
But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”

verse.text: They were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them; they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. Taking the twelve aside again, he began to tell them what was going to happen to him:

text.q: “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the scribes. They will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles,
and they will mock him and spit on him and flog him and kill him, and after three days he will rise.”

verse.text: James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.”
He said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They said to him, “Grant that we may sit, one at your right and one at your left, in your glory.”
But Jesus said to them, “You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism I am baptized with?”
verse.note: In the Jewish Scriptures 'the cup' is a common image for the portion God hands a person, often one of suffering or judgment. The verb 'baptize' in ordinary Greek could also mean to be plunged under or overwhelmed, and was used figuratively of being swamped by disaster. Both images point to the suffering and death Jesus has just predicted.

verse.text: They said to him, “We can.” Jesus said to them, “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism I am baptized with you will be baptized,

text.q: but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to grant; it is for those for whom it has been prepared.”

verse.text: When the ten heard this, they began to be indignant at James and John.
Jesus called them to him and said to them, “You know that those who are regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones wield authority over them.

text.q: But it is not so among you. Rather, whoever wants to become great among you will be your servant,
and whoever wants to be first among you will be slave of all.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is 'servant', but the Greek word meant a person owned by another, and hearers knew it. It is a step lower than the 'servant' of the previous verse, which translates a different word, so the saying intensifies. Several modern translations now use 'slave'; others keep 'servant' or 'bondservant' to avoid association with race-based chattel slavery.

text.q: For even the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

verse.note: The word was the ordinary term for the price paid to free a slave, a captive or a prisoner of war, which fits the slave language of the previous verse. 'For many' uses a preposition meaning 'in place of' or 'in exchange for'. Many scholars hear an echo of Isaiah 53 here, though this is debated.

verse.text: They came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a large crowd, Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting beside the road.
When he heard that it was Jesus the Nazarene, he began to cry out and say, “Son of David, Jesus, have mercy on me!”
Many rebuked him, telling him to be quiet, but he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” So they called the blind man, saying to him, “Take courage! Get up; he is calling you.”
He threw off his cloak, sprang up, and came to Jesus.
Jesus answered him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “Rabbouni, let me see again.”
verse.note: Mark gives the Aramaic word in Greek letters without translating it, and the text does the same. It is a heightened form of 'Rabbi', roughly 'my master' or 'my teacher'. Its only other New Testament occurrence is John 20:16, where it is glossed as 'Teacher'.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “Go; your faith has saved you.” Immediately he could see again, and he followed him on the road.
verse.note: The Greek verb covers both rescue from illness or danger and salvation in the fuller sense, and many versions render it 'made you well' here. 'Saved' is kept because it is the same verb as in the disciples' question in verse 26, 'Then who can be saved?', and Mark may intend both senses. The immediate reference is to the restoring of the man's sight.

verse.text: When they were approaching Jerusalem, at Bethphage and Bethany near the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples
and said to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and as soon as you enter it you will find a colt tied up, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it.
verse.note: The Greek word means the young of a horse or a donkey. Mark does not say which, but a donkey is almost certainly meant: Matthew and John say so, and the scene recalls Zechariah 9:9, where Jerusalem's king arrives on a donkey's colt. An animal never yet ridden was thought fitting for sacred or royal use.

text.q: And if anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord needs it, and he will send it back here right away.’”

verse.note: The Greek word can mean 'the Lord', 'the master' or 'the owner', and the phrase could be read 'its owner needs it'. Most translations take it as Jesus referring to himself as the Lord, as here. Some scholars think the wording is deliberately open, since bystanders would have heard only that someone with a claim on the animal required it.

verse.text: They went off and found a colt tied at a door, outside on the street, and they untied it.
Some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?”
They told them just as Jesus had said, and they let them go.
They brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks over it, and he sat on it.
Many spread their cloaks on the road, and others leafy branches they had cut from the fields.
Those who went ahead and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!
verse.note: The crowd's words come from Psalm 118:25–26, a psalm sung by pilgrims at the great festivals. 'Hosanna' represents a Hebrew plea meaning 'save, please'. By this period it seems also to have been used as a shout of acclamation, which is how it works here.

text.q: Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest heaven!”

verse.text: He entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. After looking around at everything, since the hour was already late, he went out to Bethany with the Twelve.
The next day, when they had left Bethany, he was hungry.
Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see whether he might find anything on it. When he came to it he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.

note.term: it was not the season for figs

verse.note: Mark's remark makes the incident deliberately puzzling as a story about hunger alone. He places the fig tree on either side of the action in the temple, and most interpreters read the two together: the tree with leaves but no fruit is an acted sign of judgment on the temple. The prophets used the barren fig tree as an image for Israel (for example Jeremiah 8:13).

verse.text: He responded by saying to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” And his disciples were listening.

They came to Jerusalem. He entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling and buying in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those who sold doves,
verse.note: The word covers the whole temple complex, not only the sanctuary building. The trading took place in its large outer court, the one area open to non-Jews. Money changers exchanged everyday coinage for the currency accepted for the temple tax, and doves were the sacrifice prescribed for those who could not afford a larger animal.

verse.text: and he would not let anyone carry anything through the temple.
He was teaching and saying to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.”
verse.note: Jesus joins Isaiah 56:7, on the temple as a house of prayer for all nations, to Jeremiah 7:11. The Greek word means a violent robber or bandit, not a petty thief or a cheat. In Jeremiah the 'den' is the hideout where robbers feel safe after their crimes, so the charge is that the temple is treated as a refuge by people who do wrong elsewhere, and not only that the trading there was dishonest.

verse.text: The chief priests and the scribes heard of it and began looking for a way to destroy him; for they were afraid of him, because the whole crowd was astonished at his teaching.
And whenever evening came, they would go out of the city.

note.term: whenever evening came, they would go out
note.traditional: when evening came, they went out

verse.note: The Greek construction can describe a repeated habit during these days in Jerusalem, as rendered here, or a single evening ('when evening came, they went out'), and translations are divided. Some manuscripts also read 'he would go out' in place of 'they'.

verse.text: As they passed by early in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered from the roots up.
Peter remembered and said to him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree you cursed has withered.”
Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'have faith of God'. Almost all interpreters take this as faith directed toward God, as translated. A minority reads it as a reference to God's own faithfulness.

text.q: Truly I tell you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in their heart but believes that what they say is happening, it will be done for them.
For this reason I tell you, whatever you pray and ask for, believe that you have received it, and it will be done for you.

note.term: believe that you have received it

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have a past tense, 'you received'. Many later manuscripts read 'you are receiving' or 'you will receive', which look like attempts to ease the surprising statement that the thing asked for should be regarded as already given. The past tense is followed here, as in most modern editions.

text.q: And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father in the heavens may also forgive you your offenses.”

verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase for God's dwelling that a first-century hearer would have recognised. Most English translations flatten it to 'in heaven'. The plural is kept here because the Greek has it.

The word means a wrong done against God or another person. 'Trespasses' is the traditional rendering, but in modern English it mainly suggests entering someone's property unlawfully. Some translations simply use 'sins', which blurs the distinction from the more common Greek word for sin.

note.term: so that your Father in the heavens may also forgive you your offenses.”

verse.note: The numbering passes from verse 25 to verse 27. Verse 26 ('But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in the heavens forgive your offenses') is absent from the earliest manuscripts and was probably added by copyists from Matthew 6:15. The Greek text translated here does not include it.

verse.text: They came again to Jerusalem. As he was walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes and the elders came to him
and said to him, “By what authority are you doing these things? Or who gave you this authority to do these things?”
Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question. Answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.

text.q: The baptism of John: was it from heaven or from people? Answer me.”

verse.note: 'Heaven' is here a reverent Jewish way of saying 'God' without using the name. The question is whether John acted on God's commission or only on human initiative. The same answer would apply to Jesus's own authority.

verse.text: They argued it out among themselves, saying, “What are we to say? If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’
But are we to say, ‘From people’?” They were afraid of the crowd, for everyone held that John really was a prophet.
So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.”
Then he began to speak to them in parables: “A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a pit for the winepress, and built a tower. Then he leased it to tenants and went abroad.
verse.note: The fence, the winepress pit and the tower echo the song of the vineyard in Isaiah 5:1–2, where the vineyard is Israel and its owner is God. A hearer who knew the Scriptures would catch the allusion and expect a story about God and his people. Leasing an estate to tenants for a share of the crop while the owner lived elsewhere was a familiar arrangement.

text.q: When the season came, he sent a slave to the tenants to collect from the tenants a share of the vineyard’s fruit.

verse.note: The Greek word means a person owned by another, and the first hearers understood it that way. “Servant” softens this and blurs the difference from other Greek words for attendants and helpers. Several modern translations now use “slave”; others keep “servant” to avoid association with race-based chattel slavery.

text.q: But they seized him, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.
Again he sent another slave to them; that one they struck on the head and treated shamefully.

verse.note: The Greek verb is extremely rare, and its meaning is inferred from its connection with the word for “head” and from the context. Most translators take it as striking or wounding the head. The exact sense remains uncertain.

text.q: He sent yet another, and that one they killed; and so with many others, beating some and killing others.
He had one left, a beloved son. Last of all he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’
So they seized him and killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.
What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others.
Have you not even read this scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone;

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 118:22–23 in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. The phrase is literally “head of the corner.” It may mean the foundation stone at a building’s corner or the capstone that completes the top of a wall or arch, and scholars are divided. On either reading the rejected stone ends up in the most important position.

text.q: this came from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?”

verse.text: They were looking for a way to arrest him, but they were afraid of the crowd, for they knew that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.
Then they sent some of the Pharisees and the Herodians to him, to trap him in what he said.

They came and said to him, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and are swayed by no one, for you pay no regard to people’s standing but teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to give the poll tax to Caesar, or not? Should we give it, or should we not?”
verse.note: The Greek borrows the Latin word census. It refers to the head tax Rome levied on a subject population on the basis of a registration, as distinct from tolls and customs. Judea had paid it since coming under direct Roman rule, and it was resented as a mark of subjection. That is why the question is a trap: a yes would alienate the crowd, and a no could be reported as sedition.

verse.text: But he, knowing their hypocrisy, said to them, “Why are you testing me? Bring me a denarius so that I may look at it.”
verse.note: A Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s wage for a labourer. The denarius of the reigning emperor Tiberius carried his portrait and an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus. Many interpreters hear in the word “image” an allusion to human beings as made in God’s image, so that what is owed to God is oneself; the text does not say this outright.

verse.text: They brought one, and he said to them, “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.”
Jesus said to them, “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” And they were utterly amazed at him.
verse.note: The questioners asked whether to “give” the tax. Jesus answers with a compound of the same verb that means to give back or to pay what is owed. “Render” once carried this sense but no longer does in ordinary English, and “give back” keeps the echo of the question.

verse.text: Then Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to him and questioned him, saying,

text.q: “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves behind a wife but leaves no child, his brother is to take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.

verse.note: The reference is to Deuteronomy 25:5–6. When a married man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son would carry on the dead man’s name. The Sadducees use this law to make resurrection look absurd, and Jesus answers them from the books of Moses, the authority they themselves appeal to.

text.q: There were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and when he died he left no offspring.
The second took her and died, leaving no offspring behind, and the third likewise.
None of the seven left offspring. Last of all, the woman also died.
In the resurrection, when they rise, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife.”

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “Is this not why you are mistaken, that you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God?

text.q: For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in the heavens.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking about God’s dwelling. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” The plural is kept here because a first-century hearer would have noticed the Semitic turn of phrase.

text.q: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God said to him, ‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’?

note.term: in the passage about the bush

verse.note: The Greek says simply “at the bush.” Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a passage was cited by a key word or subject. The reference is to the burning bush episode, and the words quoted are from Exodus 3:6. Older versions took the phrase as the place where God spoke; most modern translations take it as a citation, as here.

text.q: He is not God of the dead but of the living. You are badly mistaken.”

verse.text: One of the scribes came up and heard them debating. Seeing that Jesus had answered them well, he asked him, “Which commandment is first of all?”
Jesus answered, “The first is, ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one,

note.term: the Lord our God, the Lord is one
note.traditional: The Lord our God is one Lord

verse.note: This is Deuteronomy 6:4, the opening of the Shema, which devout Jews recited daily. The Greek, like the Hebrew behind it, has no verb in the first half and can be construed several ways, including “the Lord our God is one Lord” and “the Lord is our God, the Lord alone.” The scribe’s reply in verse 32, “he is one,” suggests the statement was heard as affirming God’s oneness.

text.q: and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’
The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”

verse.text: The scribe said to him, “Well said, Teacher. In truth you have said that he is one, and there is no other besides him;

text.q: and to love him with all one’s heart and all one’s understanding and all one’s strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is far more than all the whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.”

verse.text: Jesus, seeing that he had answered thoughtfully, said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And after that no one dared to question him any longer.
As Jesus was teaching in the temple, he spoke up and said, “How can the scribes say that the Messiah is David’s son?
verse.note: Here the Greek word is a title under discussion: the anointed king Israel expected. It is not a name for Jesus. “Messiah” conveys the title to a modern reader, while “Christ” is kept where the word functions as a name. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

text.q: David himself said by the Holy Spirit, ‘The Lord said to my lord, “Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet.”’

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 110:1. In Hebrew the first “Lord” is the divine name and the second is an ordinary word for a master or superior, while the Greek uses the same word for both. The argument assumes David is the speaker: if David calls the Messiah his superior, “son of David” cannot be the whole truth about him. Most translations capitalise both; the lower case here marks the distinction in the psalm.

verse.text: David himself calls him lord, so how can he be his son?” And the large crowd listened to him gladly.
In his teaching he said, “Watch out for the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and to be greeted in the marketplaces,

text.q: and to have the front seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.
They devour widows’ houses and, for show, pray at length. These will receive a harsher judgment.”

verse.text: He sat down opposite the treasury and watched how the crowd was putting money into the treasury. Many rich people were putting in large amounts.
Then one poor widow came and put in two tiny copper coins, which make a penny.

note.term: two tiny copper coins, which make a penny
note.traditional: two mites, which make a farthing

verse.note: The Greek names two lepta, the smallest coins in circulation in Judea, and explains their value as one quadrans, the smallest Roman coin, worth one sixty-fourth of a denarius. The explanation in Roman terms is often taken as a hint about the audience Mark wrote for. “Penny” stands for the lowest coin in use and is not an exact equivalent.

verse.text: He called his disciples to him and said to them, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all the others who are putting money into the treasury.

text.q: For they all put in out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”

verse.text: As he was going out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Teacher, look! What stones and what buildings!”
And Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone will be left here on another that will not be thrown down.”
As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John and Andrew asked him privately,

text.q: “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?”

verse.text: Jesus began to say to them, “Watch out that no one leads you astray.

text.q: Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and they will lead many astray.

verse.note: The Greek is simply 'I am' (egō eimi), the ordinary way to say 'It is I' or 'I am the one.' Here it most naturally means a claim to be the Messiah, as Matthew's parallel makes explicit. Some interpreters hear an echo of the divine self-designation 'I am' from the Greek Old Testament, but the context of impostors coming 'in my name' favours the simpler sense.

text.q: When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. It must happen, but the end is not yet.
For nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom; there will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These things are the beginning of birth pains.
As for you, watch out for yourselves. They will hand you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings because of me, as a testimony to them.
And the good news must first be proclaimed to all the nations.

verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for the public announcement of good news, used also of royal and imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' now sounds like a religious term or a book title, so the plainer rendering is used. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

text.q: When they lead you away to hand you over, do not worry beforehand about what you will say, but say whatever is given to you in that hour, for it is not you who are speaking but the Holy Spirit.
Brother will hand over brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise up against parents and put them to death.
And you will be hated by everyone because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.

verse.text: But when you see the abomination that brings desolation standing where he should not be (let the reader understand), then those in Judea must flee to the mountains;
verse.note: The phrase comes from the book of Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11), where it refers to something detestable to God that defiles the temple and leaves it desolate. 1 Maccabees 1:54 applies it to the pagan altar that Antiochus IV set up in the Jerusalem temple in 167 BC. Jesus's hearers would have understood a comparable desecration to come; what event is meant is disputed, with many connecting it to the Roman war of AD 66–70.

note.traditional: standing where it ought not to be

verse.note: 'Abomination' is a neuter noun in Greek, but the participle 'standing' is masculine, a mismatch a Greek reader would notice. It suggests the abomination is thought of as a person, or as embodied in one, and the translation reflects that with 'he.' Most English versions smooth this to 'it.' Some scholars treat the masculine as loose grammar without significance.

This is usually taken as an aside by Mark to the person reading his book aloud to a congregation, flagging the veiled reference; it is labelled here as the narrator's words. It could instead be part of Jesus's speech, addressed to the reader of Daniel. Matthew's parallel, which names Daniel, can be read either way.

text.q: the one on the housetop must not come down or go inside to take anything out of his house,
and the one in the field must not turn back to get his cloak.
Woe to those who are pregnant and those who are nursing in those days!
Pray that it may not happen in winter.
For those days will be a distress such as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be.

verse.note: The Greek word is an ordinary term for pressure, suffering or hardship. 'Tribulation' is now archaic and has become a technical term in some end-time schemes, which reads more into the word than a first-century reader would have heard. The wording echoes Daniel 12:1.

text.q: And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would have been saved. But for the sake of the chosen ones whom he chose, he has cut short the days.

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'all flesh would not have been saved,' a Semitic idiom in which 'all flesh' means every living person. 'Saved' here means surviving the distress. Most modern translations render the idiom in a similar way.

note.term: the chosen ones whom he chose

verse.note: The noun and the verb share the same root in Greek, and the repetition is deliberate. 'The elect' hides the wordplay and has become a theological term; 'chosen ones' is what the word ordinarily meant and is used throughout the chapter.

text.q: And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Messiah!’ or ‘Look, there!’ do not believe it.

verse.note: The Greek christos translates the Hebrew title 'Messiah,' the anointed king Israel expected. Here the word is plainly a title for a figure people are looking for, not a name for Jesus, so 'Messiah' is used. The 'false messiahs' of the next verse are correspondingly rendered. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

text.q: For false messiahs and false prophets will arise and will give signs and wonders in order to lead astray, if possible, the chosen ones.
But you, watch out. I have told you everything beforehand.
But in those days, after that distress, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light,

verse.note: The language of verses 24–25 is drawn from the prophets, especially Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4, where the darkening of sun, moon and stars accompanies God's judgment on nations such as Babylon and Edom. Interpreters differ on whether Jesus uses it here for literal cosmic events at the end of the age, or, as the prophets often did, as imagery for a world-shaking act of divine judgment within history.

text.q: and the stars will be falling from the sky, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.
And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.

note.term: the Son of Man coming in clouds

verse.note: The words allude to Daniel 7:13, where 'one like a son of man' comes with the clouds of heaven to God and is given everlasting dominion. Most interpreters take the verse as Jesus's return in glory. A minority reads it, with Daniel, as his vindication and enthronement, seen in the events of that generation.

text.q: And then he will send out the angels and gather the chosen ones from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.
Learn the parable from the fig tree: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near.
So you too, when you see these things happening, know that he is near, at the very doors.

note.traditional: he is near / it is near

verse.note: The Greek has no expressed subject, so 'he is near' (the Son of Man) and 'it is near' (the end, or the event just described) are both possible. English versions are divided. 'He' is chosen because the image of someone standing at the doors suits a person and the Son of Man has just been mentioned.

text.q: Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened.

verse.note: In ordinary usage, and elsewhere in Mark, the phrase means the people alive at the time of speaking. Because that raises the question of how 'all these things' happened within their lifetime, other senses have been proposed, such as 'this race' or 'this kind of people,' or the generation that sees the signs. The plain sense is the one most scholars accept for the Greek, with disagreement about what 'all these things' covers.

text.q: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
But about that day or the hour no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
Watch out, stay alert, for you do not know when the time is.

verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'stay alert and pray.' The words 'and pray' are absent from a few important early witnesses and from the SBLGNT text translated here; they may have been added under the influence of Mark 14:38.

text.q: It is like a man away on a journey, who left his house and gave his slaves authority, to each his work, and commanded the doorkeeper to stay awake.

verse.note: The Greek word means a person owned by another, and ancient hearers understood it so; in a household like this one, slaves could be entrusted with considerable responsibility. 'Servants' softens the word. Several modern translations now use 'slave,' while others keep 'servant' to avoid association with modern race-based slavery.

text.q: So stay awake, for you do not know when the master of the house is coming, whether in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or early in the morning,

note.term: whether in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or early in the morning

verse.note: These are the popular names of the four watches into which the Roman system divided the night, each about three hours long, from sunset to sunrise. The master may return during any of them, so the doorkeeper cannot count on sleeping through part of the night.

text.q: or he may come suddenly and find you sleeping.
And what I say to you I say to everyone: Stay awake.”

verse.text: Now the Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread were two days away. The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to seize him by stealth and kill him,
for they were saying, “Not during the festival, or there may be an uproar among the people.”
While he was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster jar of perfume, pure nard, very costly. She broke the jar and poured it over his head.
verse.note: The adjective describing the nard is rare and its meaning is uncertain. Most scholars take it as 'genuine' or 'unadulterated', which is followed here. Other proposals are 'liquid' and a trade name for a particular variety of the plant.

verse.text: But some were saying indignantly to one another, “Why this waste of the perfume?
This perfume could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor.” And they scolded her harshly.

note.traditional: three hundred pence; a year's wages

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day's pay for a labourer. Three hundred denarii was therefore close to a year's wages, which explains the onlookers' indignation.

verse.text: But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why are you giving her trouble? She has done a good deed for me.

text.q: For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want you can do good to them; but you do not always have me.
She did what she could: she has anointed my body ahead of time for its burial.
Truly I tell you, wherever the good news is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told, in memory of her.”

verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' now sounds like a religious term or a book title, so the plain meaning is given. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

verse.text: Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went off to the chief priests to hand him over to them.
verse.note: The verb means to hand over or deliver up, and Mark uses the same word when the priests hand Jesus to Pilate and Pilate hands him over to be crucified. Greek had a separate word for 'betray', which is not used here. Most translations use 'betray' for Judas because the act was a betrayal; 'hand over' is kept throughout this chapter so the repeated verb stays visible.

verse.text: When they heard it they were glad, and they promised to give him money. So he began looking for a good opportunity to hand him over.
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, “Where do you want us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?”
So he sent two of his disciples and told them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,

text.q: and wherever he goes in, say to the owner of the house, ‘The Teacher says: Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’
He will show you a large upstairs room, furnished and ready. Prepare for us there.”

verse.text: The disciples set out and went into the city and found things just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve.
As they were reclining and eating, Jesus said, “Truly I tell you, one of you will hand me over, one who is eating with me.”
They began to be grieved and to say to him, one after another, “Surely not I?”
He said to them, “One of the Twelve, the one dipping with me into the bowl.

text.q: For the Son of Man goes just as it is written about him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is handed over! It would be better for that man if he had not been born.”

verse.text: While they were eating, he took bread, said a blessing, broke it, gave it to them and said, “Take; this is my body.”
Then he took a cup, gave thanks and gave it to them, and they all drank from it.
He said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

text.q: Truly I tell you, I will never again drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.”

verse.text: After singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
And Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’

text.q: But after I have been raised, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”

verse.text: But Peter said to him, “Even if they all fall away, I will not.”
Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you: today, this very night, before a rooster crows twice, you yourself will deny me three times.”
But he kept insisting all the more, “Even if I must die with you, I will never deny you.” And they all said the same.
They came to a place called Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.”
He took Peter, James and John with him, and he began to be filled with dread and deep distress.
He said to them, “My soul is deeply grieved, to the point of death. Remain here and stay awake.”
Going on a little farther, he fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him.
He said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Take this cup away from me. Yet not what I want, but what you want.”
verse.note: Abba is the Aramaic word for 'father', which Mark preserves and then translates into Greek. It was used by adult children as well as small ones, so the popular claim that it means 'Daddy' is not supported by most scholars. It is intimate and direct without being childish.

verse.text: He came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Did you not have the strength to stay awake one hour?

text.q: Stay awake and pray, so that you do not come into testing. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

verse.note: The Greek word covers both a trial that tests a person's faithfulness and an enticement to sin. In this scene the disciples face an ordeal that will prove their loyalty, so 'testing' is the nearer sense. Most translations have 'temptation'; some have 'the time of trial'.

verse.text: Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words.
And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.
He came the third time and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Enough! The hour has come. Look, the Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners.
verse.note: The single Greek word here is one of the most disputed in Mark. 'It is enough' is the usual rendering, but the verb is common in receipts meaning 'paid in full', so some read it as 'the account is settled' or as a reference to Judas having received his money. The preceding words can also be read as a command or an ironic concession ('Sleep on, then') and not as a question.

text.q: Get up, let us go. Look, the one handing me over has come near.”

verse.text: Immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests, the scribes and the elders.
Now the one handing him over had given them a signal, saying, “The one I kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard.”
When he came, he went up to him at once and said, “Rabbi!” and kissed him.
They laid hands on him and seized him.
But one of those standing by drew his sword, struck the high priest’s slave and cut off his ear.
verse.note: The word meant a person owned by another, and ancient hearers understood it so; 'servant' softens this. Several modern translations now use 'slave', while others keep 'servant' to avoid associations with modern race-based slavery. For the same reason the related word in verses 66 and 69, traditionally 'servant girl' or 'maid', is rendered 'slave girl'.

verse.text: Jesus said to them in response, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest me, as if against a bandit?
verse.note: The word denotes an armed brigand who uses violence, not a thief who works by stealth, and in this period it was also applied to insurgents. That explains the swords and clubs. The same word describes the two men crucified beside Jesus in the next chapter.

text.q: Day after day I was with you in the temple, teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the scriptures be fulfilled.”

verse.text: Then they all left him and fled.
A certain young man was following him, wearing nothing but a linen cloth. They seized him,
but he left the linen cloth behind and fled naked.
They led Jesus away to the high priest, and all the chief priests, the elders and the scribes assembled.
Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the high priest’s courtyard, and he was sitting with the attendants and warming himself at the fire.
The chief priests and the whole council were looking for testimony against Jesus in order to put him to death, and they were finding none.
For many were giving false testimony against him, but their testimonies did not agree.
Then some stood up and gave false testimony against him, saying,

text.q: “We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this sanctuary made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.’”

verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both render 'temple'. The one in verse 49 means the whole temple complex with its courts; the one here means the sanctuary building itself, the dwelling place of God. 'Sanctuary' keeps the two apart.

verse.text: Yet not even so did their testimony agree.
Then the high priest stood up in their midst and questioned Jesus: “Have you no answer at all? What is it that these men are testifying against you?”
But he stayed silent and gave no answer at all. Again the high priest questioned him and said to him, “Are you the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?”
verse.note: The high priest is asking whether Jesus claims a title: the anointed king Israel expected. 'Messiah' conveys that to a modern reader, whereas 'Christ' now sounds like a name. Several modern translations use 'Messiah' where the title is the point and 'Christ' elsewhere.

verse.text: Jesus said, “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”
verse.note: 'The Power' is a reverent way of referring to God without naming him, as is 'the Blessed One' in the high priest's question. The reply combines two scriptures: the king seated at God's right hand in Psalm 110:1 and the figure 'like a son of man' who comes with the clouds of heaven in Daniel 7:13. It is this claim to share God's authority that the high priest calls blasphemy.

verse.text: The high priest tore his clothes and said, “What further need do we have of witnesses?
You have heard the blasphemy. How does it look to you?” And they all condemned him as deserving death.
Some began to spit on him, to cover his face, to strike him with their fists and to say to him, “Prophesy!” And the attendants took charge of him with slaps.
While Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the high priest’s slave girls came by.
Seeing Peter warming himself, she looked closely at him and said, “You too were with the Nazarene, Jesus.”
But he denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you are talking about.” He went outside into the forecourt, and a rooster crowed.
verse.note: These words are missing from several important early manuscripts, and some editions bracket or omit them. The SBLGNT prints them without brackets, and they prepare for the 'second time' in verse 72. Scribes may have added them to supply a first crowing, or dropped them to match the other Gospels, which mention only one.

verse.text: The slave girl saw him and began again to say to those standing by, “This man is one of them.”
But again he denied it. A little later those standing by again said to Peter, “You really are one of them, for you are a Galilean, and your speech is the same.”

note.term: and your speech is the same

verse.note: This clause is absent from the earliest manuscripts and from many critical editions and modern translations. Many scholars think it was added under the influence of Matthew 26:73. The SBLGNT includes it, so it is translated here.

verse.text: But he began to call down curses and to swear, “I do not know this man you are talking about.”
At once a rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered the word Jesus had spoken to him: “Before a rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” And he broke down and wept.

note.traditional: when he thought thereon, he wept; he broke down and wept

verse.note: The Greek participle literally means 'having thrown upon', and its sense here is uncertain. Proposals include 'when he reflected on it', 'he began to weep', 'he covered his head and wept', and 'he rushed out and wept'. 'Broke down' follows the majority of modern translations.

verse.text: As soon as it was morning, the chief priests, after consulting with the elders and scribes and the whole council, bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate.

note.traditional: the whole council / the whole Sanhedrin

verse.note: The Greek word is synedrion, the source of the name Sanhedrin: the high council in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest. It could not carry out an execution on its own authority under Roman rule, which is why Jesus is taken to Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea.

verse.text: Pilate asked him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” He answered him, “You say so.”

note.traditional: Thou sayest it / You have said so

verse.note: The reply is literally ‘You are saying [it].’ It neither plainly accepts nor plainly rejects the title. Some interpreters take it as a qualified yes (‘It is as you say’), others as a deflection (‘Those are your words’). The rendering leaves the reserve intact, and Pilate’s continued questioning suggests he did not hear a confession.

verse.text: And the chief priests were accusing him of many things.
Pilate questioned him again: “Have you no answer at all? See how many charges they are bringing against you.”
But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.
Now at the festival he used to release to them one prisoner, whichever one they requested.
The man called Barabbas was in prison with the rebels who had committed murder during the rebellion.
The crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them.
Pilate answered them, “Do you want me to release to you the king of the Jews?”
For he knew that it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed him over.
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas to them instead.
Pilate spoke to them again: “Then what do you want me to do with the one you call the king of the Jews?”
They shouted back, “Crucify him!”
Pilate said to them, “Why? What wrong has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Crucify him!”
Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas to them, and after having Jesus flogged, he handed him over to be crucified.
The soldiers led him away inside the palace, that is, the governor’s headquarters, and called together the whole cohort.
verse.note: Mark uses the Latin word praetorium, the official residence and headquarters of a Roman governor. In Jerusalem this was either Herod’s former palace or the Antonia fortress beside the temple; which one is disputed. A cohort was nominally about six hundred soldiers, though the term may be used loosely here for the unit on duty.

verse.text: They dressed him in purple, and after weaving a crown of thorns they put it on him.
And they began to salute him: “Hail, king of the Jews!”
They kept striking his head with a reed and spitting on him, and going down on their knees they paid him homage.
When they had finished mocking him, they stripped him of the purple and put his own clothes on him. Then they led him out to crucify him.
They pressed into service a passer-by, a certain Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, who was coming in from the country, to carry his cross.
verse.note: The verb was the regular term for the right of officials and soldiers to requisition a civilian’s labour or animals on the spot. ‘Compelled’ is accurate but loses the sense of a recognised, legal imposition by an occupying army. The condemned normally carried the crossbeam himself; Mark does not say why Jesus did not.

verse.text: They brought him to the place Golgotha, which translated means Place of the Skull.
They tried to give him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it.
And they crucified him and divided his clothes among themselves, casting lots for them to decide who would take what.
It was the third hour when they crucified him.
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about nine in the morning, the sixth (verse 33) about noon, and the ninth about three in the afternoon. Many modern translations convert to clock times; the ancient reckoning is kept here because the hours were approximate divisions of daylight, not clock readings.

verse.text: The inscription stating the charge against him read: “The King of the Jews.”
And with him they crucified two bandits, one on his right and one on his left.
verse.note: The word means an armed brigand who uses violence, not a thief, for which Greek has a different word. The Jewish historian Josephus uses it for insurgents against Rome, and since Barabbas and his fellow rebels have just been mentioned, these two may have been condemned for rebellion. Several modern translations have ‘bandits’ or ‘rebels’.

note.term: one on his right and one on his left

verse.note: There is no verse 28 in this edition. The sentence found there in later manuscripts (‘And the scripture was fulfilled that says, He was counted among the lawless’) is absent from the earliest witnesses and was probably added under the influence of Luke 22:37. Most modern editions omit it while keeping the traditional verse numbers.

verse.text: Those passing by hurled abuse at him, shaking their heads and saying, “Ha! You who would destroy the temple and build it in three days,

text.q: save yourself and come down from the cross!”

verse.text: In the same way the chief priests too, along with the scribes, were mocking him among themselves and saying, “He saved others; himself he cannot save!
Let the Messiah, the king of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!” Even those crucified with him were taunting him.
verse.note: The Greek is ho christos, ‘the anointed one’, used here with the article as a title and set beside ‘the king of Israel’. A first-century Jewish hearer heard a royal title, not a name, which ‘Messiah’ conveys better than ‘Christ’. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

verse.text: When the sixth hour came, darkness fell over the whole land until the ninth hour.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean a particular land or region, or the earth as a whole. Most translations take it as the land of Judea, as here; ‘over the whole earth’ is equally possible grammatically.

verse.text: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which translated means, “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?”
verse.note: Jesus cries out the opening line of Psalm 22, which Mark gives first in Aramaic and then in Greek. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for leaving someone behind or in the lurch; ‘forsaken’ is the traditional rendering but is now archaic, and several modern translations use ‘abandoned’. The Aramaic ‘Eloi’ explains how bystanders could mishear a call to Elijah.

verse.text: Some of those standing by heard it and said, “Look, he is calling Elijah.”
Someone ran, filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Wait! Let us see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”
verse.note: The word refers to the cheap, sharp wine drunk by soldiers and labourers, not to vinegar in the modern sense. Most modern translations render it ‘sour wine’ or ‘wine vinegar’. Many interpreters see an echo of Psalm 69:21, where the sufferer is given this drink for his thirst.

verse.text: But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed his last.
And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
When the centurion who stood facing him saw that he breathed his last in this way, he said, “Truly this man was God’s Son!”
verse.note: The Greek has no article: ‘son of God’. On a Roman soldier’s lips this could mean ‘a son of a god’, a divine or heroic figure. Greek grammar also allows a definite sense when such a phrase precedes the verb, and Mark’s readers would hear the title the Gospel itself gives Jesus. The rendering keeps the wording open to both.

verse.text: There were also women watching from a distance, among them Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome,
who had followed him and served him when he was in Galilee, and many other women who had come up with him to Jerusalem.
When evening had already come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath,
Joseph of Arimathea came, a respected councillor who was himself also waiting for the kingdom of God. Gathering his courage, he went in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
Pilate was amazed that he should already be dead, and summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he had been dead for some time.
When he learned it from the centurion, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
Joseph bought a linen cloth, took him down, wrapped him in the cloth, and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of rock; then he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching where he was laid.
When the Sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they could go and anoint him.
And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen.

note.term: the first day of the week
note.traditional: the first day of the week

verse.note: Literally ‘on day one of the sabbaths.’ In Jewish Greek the plural ‘sabbaths’ could mean the week, and days were counted from the Sabbath, so this is the day after it, our Sunday. The Sabbath had ended at sunset the evening before, when the spices could be bought; the women come at first light.

verse.text: They were saying to one another, “Who will roll the stone away from the entrance of the tomb for us?”
And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, for it was extremely large.
Entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verse.note: Mark calls the figure simply a young man, and the translation keeps that. White clothing was the conventional dress of heavenly messengers in Jewish writing, and Matthew's parallel account calls him an angel outright. Nearly all interpreters take Mark to mean an angel, so his words are labelled as an angel's speech.

verse.text: But he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here. Look, here is the place where they laid him.

note.traditional: He is risen / He has risen

verse.note: The Greek verb is passive in form. It can be read as a true passive, ‘he has been raised’ (that is, by God), or as an intransitive, ‘he has risen’; translations divide. The passive is chosen here because early Christian proclamation regularly says that God raised Jesus, but the other reading remains grammatically possible.

text.q: But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.’”

verse.text: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. ⟦And they briefly reported all that they had been commanded to Peter and those with him. And after this Jesus himself also sent out through them, from east to west, the sacred and imperishable proclamation of eternal salvation. Amen.⟧

note.term: And they briefly reported all that they had been commanded to Peter and those with him

verse.note: The double brackets mark text that the editors of the Greek edition judge not to be original to Mark. The two earliest Greek manuscripts of Mark, both from the fourth century, end at ‘for they were afraid.’ The bracketed sentences here, known as the shorter ending, appear in a small number of manuscripts, usually followed by verses 9–20, and their vocabulary is unlike Mark's. Whether Mark meant to end at ‘for they were afraid’ or an original ending was lost is disputed.
The adverb can mean ‘concisely’ (of speech) or ‘promptly’ (of time). English translations divide between the two, and either fits the sentence.

Literally ‘those around Peter.’ In Greek of this period the idiom commonly includes the named person together with his circle, and it is rendered that way here. Some translations keep the literal wording, which could be heard as leaving Peter out.

verse.text: ⟦Now after he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had driven out seven demons.

note.term: Now after he rose early on the first day of the week

verse.note: The double brackets around verses 9–20, the longer ending, mark them as a later addition in the editors' judgment. They are found in the great majority of manuscripts and were known by the late second century, but they are absent from the two earliest Greek manuscripts, and Eusebius and Jerome report that they were missing from most copies known to them. The style differs from the rest of Mark, and Mary Magdalene is introduced as if for the first time. Most scholars regard the passage as an early summary of resurrection appearances attached to the Gospel.

verse.text: She went and reported it to those who had been with him, as they were mourning and weeping.
And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe it.
After this he showed himself in a different form to two of them as they were walking, on their way into the country.
And they went back and reported it to the rest; but they did not believe them either.

Later he showed himself to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had been raised.
And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.
verse.note: ‘Gospel’ is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between ‘good news’ and ‘gospel.’

text.q: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new languages;

verse.note: The Greek word means the tongue as an organ and, by extension, a language; ‘tongues’ in the traditional rendering is simply older English for ‘languages.’ ‘Languages’ is used here because ‘tongues’ has become a technical religious term. What kind of speech is meant, whether foreign languages as in Acts 2 or the ecstatic speech discussed in 1 Corinthians, is left open by the Greek.

text.q: they will pick up snakes, and if they drink anything deadly it will not harm them at all; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will get well.”

verse.text: So then the Lord Jesus, after speaking to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.

note.term: sat down at the right hand of God

verse.note: The seat at a king's right hand was the place of highest honour and shared authority. The wording echoes Psalm 110:1 (‘Sit at my right hand’), the Scripture text most often applied to Jesus by the first Christians, and ‘taken up into heaven’ recalls the language used of Elijah.

verse.text: And they went out and proclaimed everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word through the signs that followed.⟧
